layout.title: How to Calculate Your Calorie Needs? Complete Guide
layout.intro: Your calorie needs depend on your basal metabolic rate (BMR), activity level and goal — weight loss, maintenance or muscle building. This guide explains step by step how to calculate your individual calorie needs using scientific methods.

schema.headline: How to Calculate Your Calorie Needs? Complete Guide
schema.description: Learn how to calculate your individual calorie needs — from BMR and TDEE to calorie deficit and bulking.

body.text: BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate, basal metabolism) is the calories your body burns at complete rest — only to keep the heart, brain and organs running. It is the foundation for all calorie calculations.

text.text: The most widely used and validated formula for most adults is Mifflin-St Jeor:

body.text: Weight in kg, height in cm, age in years.
Step 2: Calculate your TDEE with activity factor
TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is your total calorie need — BMR multiplied by your PAL factor (Physical Activity Level).

rows: Office or home work, little daily movement, no training
Light exercise 1–3 days/week, e.g. walks, yoga or gym in spare time
Regular exercise 3–5 days/week with moderate intensity, e.g. running or strength training
Hard training almost every day (6–7 days/week) or physically active work
Heavy physical work combined with daily intense training, e.g. elite athletes or construction workers who also train

text.text: Example: A person, 30 years old, 80 kg, 180 cm, trains 3–5 times/week (moderately active).

body.text: Eat 300–500 kcal below your TDEE. That gives about 0.3–0.5 kg of weight loss per week — slow enough to preserve muscle mass. Combine with adequate protein (1.6–2.2 g/kg) for best results.
Eat 200–400 kcal above your TDEE. That creates a small surplus for muscle growth with minimal fat gain. More than 500 kcal/day in surplus often leads to unnecessary fat storage.
Match your TDEE. Great during rest periods, rehabilitation or to stabilise weight after a longer phase.
Why doesn't the calculator always match?
TDEE calculators provide an estimate with a margin of error of typically ±10–15%. Factors that affect the real value:

items: Thyroid hormones and other hormonal balance
Thermic effect of food (proteins require more energy to digest)
Adaptive thermogenesis (body lowers metabolism during prolonged calorie deficit)

text.text: Use the calculator as a starting point. Monitor your weight for 2–3 weeks and adjust the calorie goal if you don't see the expected result.

faq.question: How do you calculate your calorie needs?
faq.answer: You calculate calorie needs in three steps: 1) Calculate your BMR (basal metabolic rate) using the Mifflin-St Jeor formula based on weight, height, age and gender. 2) Multiply BMR by an activity factor (PAL 1.2–1.9) to get TDEE — your actual calorie needs per day. 3) Adjust for your goal: eat below TDEE for weight loss, above for bulking, or match it to maintain weight.

faq.question: How many calories does a woman need per day?
faq.answer: The average woman needs 1,800–2,200 kcal/day depending on age, height, weight and activity level. This is not an exact number — individual calorie needs can differ by 400–600 kcal between two women of the same body weight if they have different activity levels. Use the TDEE calculator for your individual figure.

faq.question: How many calories does a man need per day?
faq.answer: The average man needs 2,200–2,800 kcal/day. Just like for women, it varies significantly with activity level, muscle mass and age. A sedentary man at 70 kg might have a TDEE of 1,900 kcal, while an actively training man at 90 kg might have a TDEE of 3,200 kcal.

faq.question: What happens if you eat too little?
faq.answer: If you eat too little for a long time (significantly below TDEE) you risk: muscle mass loss as the body breaks down muscle for energy, adaptive thermogenesis where BMR drops, nutritional deficiency if the calorie amount doesn't cover essential vitamins and minerals, and hormonal disruptions (lower leptin, testosterone, thyroid hormones). A moderate calorie deficit of 300–500 kcal/day is sustainable; extreme restriction is not.
